extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners in physics, biology, and philosophy of science (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the scientific validity and proper use of conceptual models (mechanism, force, atom, germ-plasm) in physics and biology; emphasizes avoiding metaphysical projection and requiring perceptual grounding. Useful for assessing whether theoretical constructs legitimately describe phenomena or improperly assert metaphysical reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as conceptual description, not metaphysical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is the description in conceptual shorthand (never the explanation) of the routine of our perceptual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat scientific theories as providing metaphysical 'whys' behind phenomena. The author repeatedly stresses that projecting conceptual machinery into reality (treating it as an account of ultimate causes) is to confuse scientific description with metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity criterion: brief summary without internal contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Any biological concept will be scientifically valid if it enables us to briefly summarise without internal contradiction any range of our perceptual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an operational test: a concept's scientific worth lies in its ability to summarize observed sequences of sense-impressions concisely and coherently. If it fails to do so or introduces contradictions, it is not scientifically valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not project conceptual constructs as phenomenal realities without perceptual equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: When a scientist asserts the phenomenal existence of concepts (e.g., atom, molecule, gemmule, germ-plasm) without a perceptual equivalent, he passes from science into metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such constructs as useful conceptual shorthand until and unless perceptual evidence identifies them; absence of direct detection is not disproof of a concept but is an argument against asserting it as a real substratum of sense-impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms precisely before applying laws (clarity of reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying laws (e.g., Newton's laws) one must specify what is meant by terms like 'body', 'particle', and identify which point or part of a body is meant when speaking of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguities (e.g., which point of a body changes motion 'in a straight line') undermine the applicability of general laws. Always ask what individual thing is conceptualised as moving, what is the relevant field, and how its motion is measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'force' as a measure, not as an ontological cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Force is seen to be a certain convenient measure of motion, and not its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'force' as an explanation of phenomena; instead treat it as a useful quantification within the conceptual model. This reframing reduces metaphysical inference from the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about extending mechanical (physical) shorthand to biology
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem is whether the conceptual shorthand of the physicist (ether, atom, molecule) will or will not also suffice to describe the biologist's perceptions of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using physical shorthand to describe life, explicitly test whether it actually summarizes biological sense-impressions; do not assume transferability. If inadequate, restate the question rather than assume mechanism explains life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical language (eternity, indestructibility) in scientific argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'eternity' and 'indestructibility' are idle phrases in the field of noumena and relate to metaphysical dogma rather than scientific concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformulate or discard metaphysical locutions when making scientific claims; base claims on perceptual groupings and observable transformations instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dogmatically assert general mechanical principles for all scales (atoms, corpuscles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The customary statements as to the superposition and combination of forces may not be scientifically correct when applied to atoms and molecules; the parallelogram of forces cannot be dogmatically asserted of corpuscles of all types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question blanket application of macroscopic mechanical principles at microscopic scales and recognize the possibility of 'modified action' where interactions differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: When borrowing terminology figuratively, re-define it or indicate intended sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of physical terms in biology often occurs 'with scarcely accurate definition' and such terms must either be re-defined or indicated as figurative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a biologist uses terms like 'force', 'unit-mass', 'molecular stimuli' figuratively, explicitly state the intended meaning or provide a re-definition to avoid conflation with physical usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for mechanistic explanation of life: sufficiency of conceptual shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Life as mechanism would mean that the physicist's conceptual shorthand suffices to describe biological sequences of sense-impressions; whether this is so must be tested, not assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To claim life is a mechanism, demonstrate that the same conceptual apparatus (atoms, forces, motions) briefly and without contradiction summarizes biological observations. Otherwise, the claim risks metaphysical projection.
